name: SQLite
summary: A complete SQL database in a library and a single file, with no server to run.
intro: SQLite is not a server. It is a library, under 900 KiB with every feature, that your program links in and calls directly. The whole database (tables, indexes, triggers, views) lives in one ordinary file that you can copy, email or check into a test fixture. Opening the database is opening the file, so there is no network hop, no user accounts and nothing to configure. Its authors describe it as a replacement for `fopen()`, not for Oracle.

It still gives you real SQL and ACID transactions that survive power loss. In write-ahead-log (WAL) mode, readers and a writer work at the same time, but only one writer can commit at a time per file. A database can reach 281 TB, the file format works across platforms, and the developers promise to support it through 2050. It is the most widely deployed database in the world, inside phones, browsers, cars and desktop apps, and it serves many small to medium websites.
strengths: Zero administration: no server, no ports, no accounts
Queries run in-process, so there’s no network round trip
One portable file is easy to back up, ship and test against
Public domain, heavily tested, with a stable file format
limits: One writer at a time per database file, so write-heavy multi-user apps outgrow it
All processes must be on one machine; WAL mode doesn’t work over a network file system
No built-in replication, user accounts or network access; separate tools have to add them, and forks such as libSQL and Turso add replicas, sync and concurrent writers
Types are flexible by default, so a column accepts values of other types unless you use `STRICT` tables

snippet.title: An embedded database with Python’s standard library
source: con = sqlite3.connect("app.db")              # creates the file if needed
con.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL")       # readers don't block the writer
con.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS notes (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, body TEXT NOT NULL)")
with con:                                    # one transaction, committed on exit
for note_id, body in con.execute("SELECT id, body FROM notes ORDER BY id"):

story: In 2000, D. Richard Hipp was leading a team writing damage-control software for a US Navy guided-missile destroyer, as a contractor. The software used an Informix database server, and when that server went down the application wouldn’t run; a dialog box popped up saying “Can’t connect to database server.” On a warship that has taken battle damage, that is the last thing the crew should see. Hipp asked why the program needed a server at all, instead of reading its data straight off the disk, and found no SQL engine that worked that way.

When a budget fight paused government contracts that year, he had a few months free and wrote one. SQLite began as a Tcl extension; version 1.0 came out in August 2000, storing data with gdbm. Version 2.0 in September 2001 replaced gdbm with Hipp’s own B-tree, and version 3.0 followed in June 2004, made possible in part by developers at AOL.

Phone makers came next: Motorola, then Symbian, which chose SQLite after a bake-off against nine other engines, then the team building Android. Shipping on millions of devices exposed bugs, so Hipp adopted the aviation software standard DO-178B and spent a year of 60-hour weeks writing tests until every branch was covered. Today SQLite is likely used more than all other database engines combined.

choices.choice: A library inside the program, not a server
choices.why: The Informix outages showed that a separate server is one more thing that can fail. SQLite was designed to run without installing a database system or needing an administrator.

choices.choice: Compile SQL into bytecode for a small virtual machine
choices.why: Hipp had built compilers before, so he treated each SQL statement as a program: a compiler translates it into bytecode, and a small engine runs that bytecode.
SQLite started as a Tcl extension, and Tcl is dynamically typed, so a column accepts values of other types. `STRICT` tables, which reject mismatches, arrived only in 2021.

choices.choice: Public domain, every line written from scratch
choices.why: With no licence terms at all, anyone can ship SQLite in anything. To keep it that way, every contributor signs a public-domain dedication, and patches from anyone else aren’t accepted.

timeline.text: Hipp writes SQLite; version 1.0 is released in August
Version 2.0 replaces gdbm with its own B-tree
Version 3.0 arrives in June, supported in part by AOL
SQLite turns 25 with version 3.50.0 in May
